sections.description: Walks through the patient’s presentation, rapid recognition of anaphylaxis, and first-line ED management, highlighting key decisions that set up the later ICU course.
subtopics: Patient profile: woman in her 60s; comorbidities (T2DM, HTN, psoriasis, depression); medications; weight 104 kg; prior mild beta-lactam reaction; large local wasp reaction
Trigger/timeline: first-ever dose of clarithromycin; symptom onset at ~1 hour; progressive pruritus, flushing, throat tightness; hypotension and hypoxemia on arrival
Clinical diagnosis of anaphylaxis: hypotension plus widespread urticaria/flushing after likely allergen; ruling-in features vs mimics (panic, vasovagal, sepsis, isolated angioedema)
Initial treatment: immediate IM epinephrine (auto-injector 0.3 mg), oxygen, IV fluids, H1 antihistamine; cessation of the offending drug
Early response and disposition: prompt improvement; admission to closely monitored setting; recognition of risk for relapse prompting continued observation

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology and phenotypes of complex anaphylaxis
sections.description: Provides mechanistic context for biphasic/multiphasic anaphylaxis and clarifies terminology used to interpret this patient’s relapsing course.
subtopics: Core biology: mast cell/basophil activation; mediators (histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, prostaglandins) causing vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchospasm, mucocutaneous signs
Why reactions can be biphasic/multiphasic: late-phase cellular recruitment, renewed mediator synthesis, continued allergen absorption/depot effect, waning epinephrine effect vs true second wave

Definitions: biphasic (recurrence after asymptomatic interval without re-exposure), multiphasic (≥2 recurrences), refractory (insufficient response to correct epinephrine), protracted (single episode > hours)
Epidemiology/timing: biphasic incidence ~4–6%; most within 24 h but up to 72–78 h reported
Risk factors for biphasic or severe courses: delayed first epinephrine, severe initial presentation, need for multiple epinephrine doses, comorbid mast cell disorders
Drug-induced anaphylaxis with macrolides: uncommon but possible; first-dose reactions may reflect prior cross-sensitization or non–IgE-mediated activation
Why this case is multiphasic, not refractory: discrete asymptomatic intervals and full responses to IM epinephrine between four distinct episodes; decreasing severity over time

sections.section_title: Diagnostic workup and etiologic reasoning, including mast cell disease
sections.description: Details the structured evaluation to confirm anaphylaxis, identify the culprit, exclude alternative explanations for relapse, and assess for an underlying mast cell disorder.
subtopics: Culprit assessment: clarithromycin as most likely trigger (temporal relationship; first dose); clindamycin rash 5 days earlier suggests delayed exanthem rather than immediate-type sensitivity; limited macrolide cross-reactivity
Excluding pseudo-biphasic causes: no further clarithromycin exposure; consider ongoing absorption vs sustained-release formulations vs retained allergen—unlikely here
Differential considerations: sepsis, ACE-inhibitor–associated angioedema (not on ACEi), anxiety/panic—clinical features and hypotension favor anaphylaxis

Tryptase strategy: recommended sampling (as soon as feasible; 1–2 h, within 4 h, after onset; and ≥24 h after resolution for baseline); interpret using the ‘20% + 2’ rule (acute > 1.2 × baseline + 2 μg/L)
Case pitfalls and interpretation: samples not timed ideally; nonetheless, elevated event and baseline tryptase support mast cell activation and persistently elevated baseline

Systemic mastocytosis workup: WHO criteria overview (major: multifocal dense mast cell infiltrates in marrow/other tissues; minors: KIT D816V mutation, aberrant CD25/CD2 on mast cells, atypical morphology, baseline tryptase >20 μg/L); tests to pursue (bone marrow with immunophenotyping and KIT mutation; serum tryptase trend)
Ancillary findings consistent with mast cell disease: hepatomegaly, neuropsychiatric symptoms; linkage with severe anaphylaxis risk even without meeting full SM criteria
Risk stratification for observation: severe presentation, multiple epinephrine doses, elevated tryptase, suspected mast cell disorder—all argue for prolonged monitored care

sections.section_title: Acute management of recurrent/multiphasic anaphylaxis in ED/ICU
sections.description: Explains evidence-based treatment priorities, dosing nuances, and monitoring for relapsing episodes, and reconciles them with choices made in this case.
subtopics: Epinephrine as first-line: adult dosing 0.01 mg/kg IM up to 0.5 mg in anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 minutes if needed; in a 104 kg adult, 0.5 mg per dose is appropriate
Auto-injector dosing pitfalls: many adults receive 0.3 mg; association with greater need for escalation vs initial 0.5 mg; strategy to ensure correct dosing in clinical settings

When to start IV epinephrine infusion: indications (refractory or rapidly recurrent episodes despite appropriate IM dosing), typical starting rates and ICU monitoring needs; risks vs benefits weighed in this patient as severity waned
Adjuncts and supportive care: high-flow oxygen, aggressive isotonic fluids for distributive shock; inhaled beta-agonists for bronchospasm; consider glucagon if on beta-blockers (not applicable here)

Role and limits of antihistamines and corticosteroids: H1/H2 for cutaneous symptoms only; current evidence does not support steroids to prevent biphasic reactions and suggests potential harm; aligning local protocols with contemporary guidance

Monitoring and disposition: continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, serial vitals and pulse oximetry, readiness for repeat IM epinephrine; prolonged observation (often 12–24 h after last episode) in high-risk patients
Interdisciplinary coordination: early allergology input; ICU involvement for multiphasic courses and consideration of vasopressor infusions

sections.section_title: Discharge planning, long-term management, and clinical lessons
sections.description: Outlines safe transition of care, long-term risk reduction, and high-yield takeaways and practice pearls drawn from the case.
subtopics: Discharge equipment and education: prescribe and teach use of epinephrine auto-injectors; consider 0.5 mg device for adults >50 kg where available; advise carrying two devices; provide written action plan

Medication and avoidance: document clarithromycin/macrolide allergy; select alternative antibiotics for future infections in context of beta-lactam allergy; avoid potential co-factors (NSAIDs, alcohol, heat, exertion) around triggers

Chronic symptom control in suspected mast cell disease: daily non-sedating H1 ± H2 antihistamines; consider leukotriene receptor antagonists; escalate to omalizumab in recurrent idiopathic/mast cell–mediated anaphylaxis per specialist

Follow-up and further evaluation: allergology/hematology referral; repeat baseline tryptase; complete bone marrow evaluation (immunophenotype, KIT mutation) if indicated; monitor organ involvement (liver, bone, GI)
Observation guidance for future events: risk-stratified monitoring durations; emphasize early, correctly dosed IM epinephrine to reduce severity and potential biphasic risk

Practice pearls: avoid epinephrine underdosing; obtain properly timed serial tryptase; consider IV epinephrine infusion for refractory/recurrent cases; update protocols to de-emphasize routine steroids; recognize mast cell disorders as key modifiers of risk
Research gaps and systems-level needs: standardized definitions, registries for biphasic/multiphasic cases, and expert consensus to guide observation and infusion strategies
